claim: Permit.io's core product is full-stack authorization-as-a-service: a cloud control plane (no-code policy editor, projects/environments, audit logs) plus self-hostable policy decision points (PDPs); 2025-26 positioning re-centers on access control for AI agents (MCP Gateway, 'real-time, fine-grained authorization at every hop'), with RBAC/ABAC/ReBAC 'out of the box' and claims of 'sub-millisecond decision latency' and SOC 2 Type II.
page_title: Permit.io — Home (AI agent access control positioning)
notes: Homepage names Cisco, Intel, BP, Palo Alto as users; marketing claims cross-checked against docs elsewhere in this ledger.

claim: permit.check() is 'the main Authorize function to enforce permissions': synchronous evaluation of (user, action, resource[, tenant, context]) returning a boolean; resource can be a type or a specific instance; the same check is exposed via the PDP REST /allowed endpoint plus /allowed/bulk, /user-permissions and /authorized_users query endpoints.
notes: Return value is allow/deny boolean; no native third 'review' outcome in the decision API itself.

claim: Just-in-time (JIT) attributes can be passed dynamically inside permit.check() on both user and resource objects (documented example: user attributes {location: 'England'}, resource attributes {hasApproval: 'true'}, tenant 'companyB'), letting callers supply arbitrary pre-declared attributes at decision time without storing them.
notes: Mechanism by which external signals (geo, risk, KYC results) could be injected into decisions; Permit itself supplies no such signals.

claim: Official docs claim local/edge PDP policy enforcement at '<10ms on p95' and policy update propagation at '~100ms on P95' (eventual consistency), with supporting material describing thousands of authorization decisions per second at sub-millisecond latency for well-configured local PDPs.
notes: Numbers are vendor-published, not independently benchmarked; corroborated on docs.permit.io/overview/local-authorization-microservice/.

claim: Two PDP deployment models: managed Cloud PDP (cloudpdp.api.permit.io; RBAC/ReBAC only — no ABAC, no custom OPA bundles, no custom data sources) and self-hosted Edge/container PDP (sidecar, centralized, clustered, or sharded) required for ABAC, custom data, read-your-own-writes, and low in-network latency; PDP supports OpenID AuthZen evaluation endpoints and response caching with TTL.
page_title: Permit's PDP (Policy Decision Point) | Permit.io Documentation
notes: Cloud PDP limitations confirmed at docs.permit.io/concepts/pdp/cloud-pdp-capabilities/: 'Use the container PDP when you need ABAC today.'

claim: OPAL (Open Policy Administration Layer), created and maintained by Permit.io, is an Apache-2.0 open-source layer (~5,500 GitHub stars) that 'detects changes to both policy and policy data in realtime, and pushes live updates to your agents' (OPA, Cedar), tracking Git repos, APIs, databases, S3, and third-party SaaS as policy/data sources; Permit's PDP and SDKs are also open source.
notes: Star count and Apache-2.0 license verified on github.com/permitio (OPAL 5,499 stars; PDP in Rust, Apache-2.0).

claim: Permit's documented ABAC examples are explicitly jurisdiction/location-shaped: 'Employees that are based within the European Union can perform any action on GDPR Protected Document', and condition examples include environment.location {'in': ['US', 'Canada']} — i.e., the mechanism for encoding jurisdiction-conditional rules exists, authored entirely by the customer.
notes: No jurisdiction content, legal interpretation, or location detection is provided by Permit; the location value must be supplied by the caller.

claim: Temporal access is modeled via ABAC condition sets comparing expiration timestamps: a time_based_groups user attribute holds {role, tenant, expires} objects and the condition checks 'expires greater-than-equals {ref: user.current_time}'; docs state 'The current_time value must be passed in permit.check() as a user attribute', so clock/effective-date logic lives in caller code, not the platform.
page_title: Time Based Role Example | Permit.io Documentation
notes: No native effective-dating of policy rules (e.g., 'rule active from Jan 1') is documented; temporal logic is a hand-built ABAC pattern.

claim: The Policy Editor is a low-code UI over resources (protected objects), actions, and roles; ticking a role/action/resource checkbox grants permission, and on save 'the Policy Editor automatically generates corresponding Rego or Cedar code', committed to a Git repository when GitOps is enabled; direct Rego/Cedar authoring is also supported.
notes: UI model is allow-grant based; see PERMITIO-039 for deny/priority limitations.

claim: ReBAC support: instance-level roles (Resource#Role), relationship tuples between resource instances, and role derivations ('a user with role Admin on a Folder... will also get an implicit assignment of Editor to all the File resource instances related to that folder'), enabling org>folder>file style hierarchies.
notes: Relevant to modeling per-instance approval relationships (e.g., transfer:transfer-1#Reviewer used by Elements approval flows).

claim: Organizational hierarchy is Workspace (org) > Projects (one per product/offering) > Environments ('logical silos for policies and data', e.g. production vs staging); environments can be 'created from scratch or copied from an existing environment'; each environment has its own secret API key used by PDPs and SDKs; member roles and permissions can be granted per project or per environment.
notes: Foundation of the control-plane model; multi-tenancy of end-customers is separate (tenants inside an environment).

claim: GitOps: 'the policy code generated by the policy-editor is saved into a Git repository before being deployed to your PDP', with a branch-per-environment model; docs promote 'adding tests, benchmarks, code-reviews, and adding more manual code' as 'all the checks and balances you need before merging changes between Git branches', giving full git-native policy version history and rollback.
notes: Historical policy versions therefore exist as git commits in the customer's own repo; approval of policy changes is delegated to the customer's git/PR tooling, not a Permit-native approval workflow.

claim: Two audit log types: basic audit logs ('actions in regards to your policy rules', i.e., permission grants/changes/revocations) and per-check decision logs — 'every time a permission check takes place... we also provide a detailed decision log' capturing user, action, resource, tenant, result and a human-readable reason (e.g., "user '...' does not match any rule that grants him the 'delete' permission..."); logs filterable by user, date, decision, tenant; the query API returns max 10,000 results; Permit 'periodically removes old logs' with extended retention via support.
notes: FAQ additionally documents activity-log querying via timestamp_from/timestamp_to with deduplication by unique log entry IDs. Retention is plan-based (14 days on free tier per pricing page).

claim: Decision-log Debug Mode adds 'why a decision was made', 'which policy was taken into consideration for the evaluation process', and 'what are the policies currently configured in your environment' to each decision log; enabled via PDP_DEBUG env var or API; docs warn 'Turning on Debug Mode will impact policy evaluation latency' and recommend disabling in production.
notes: Closest feature to per-decision policy-state capture; production-latency caveat weakens it as an always-on evidence mechanism.

claim: Audit Log Replay API (POST /v2/audit-log-replay) re-executes historical permit.check() requests against a chosen PDP; documented use cases include 'Verify that policy changes don't break existing permissions', 'Reproduce issues by replaying the exact request patterns from a specific time period', load testing, and performance analysis; constraints: replay window max 30 days, concurrency capped at 10 (more via support), and 'Always target test PDPs—never production systems.'
page_title: Stress Test the PDP | Permit.io Documentation
notes: This is replay of recorded inputs against a (possibly changed) policy — a pre-rollout impact-analysis primitive — not point-in-time reconstruction of what an old policy version decided; that requires combining with GitOps history (inference).

claim: Documented authorization-testing methodology: unit tests of policy code (e.g., OPA CLI), application/integration tests against a PDP synced to a dev environment, and CI/CD automation — 'Automated tests can be configured to run as part of the CI/CD pipeline, ensuring that every change is vetted before it goes live', including mandatory test passage before environment merges.
notes: Testing is orchestrated by the customer's CI tooling around Permit APIs; no built-in one-click policy simulation/diff report is documented.

claim: Policy lifecycle CI/CD: 'every environment is automatically deployed to PDPs mapped to them (via their API secret key)' with CD via OPAL; two documented flows — Staging (copy-env API into a staging environment, test, merge to production) and recommended Preview Branches ('dynamically create an environment for each policy pull-request' via create-env + copy-env, then merge after testing), with per-developer access restriction to preview environments.
page_title: Manage Policy Life Cycle - CI/CD | Permit.io Documentation
notes: A generic promote-through-environments deployment workflow exists; roles in it are engineering roles — no legal/counsel-specific approval construct.

claim: Operation Approval element: end users 'submit operation approvals using a dedicated user interface embedded in your application' (must 'provide a reason for the request'); creating the element auto-creates two roles — 'Reviewer' ('permission to review, approve and deny requests') and 'Approved' (the 'operate' permission); reviewers approve/deny via the Approval Management element; 'A webhook will be triggered to notify your application about the approval or denial of the request'; documented example is bank fund-transfer approval (transfer:transfer-1#Reviewer).
notes: This is runtime human-in-the-loop approval of end-user actions (a 'review' path for regulated operations), not approval of policy changes.

claim: Permit Elements are prebuilt embeddable UI components — User Management, Audit Logs, and Approval Flows ('monitor, control and approve decisions made against policies in real-time') — that can be embedded in a customer's app with brand styling and webhook configuration, 'allowing you to safely delegate them to your end users.'
notes: Audit-log element lets customers expose decision history to their own users/admins.

claim: Workspace member governance: members are assigned Workspace Owner ('can create new roles, resources and policies... change workspace settings and invite new members'), Workspace Editor (create/edit but cannot manage members), or Workspace Viewer ('can only view roles, resources and policies'); a member 'can have access to an entire workspace, or... individual projects and/or environments' with different roles per project/environment.
notes: Direct fetch returned 503; content corroborated via search-indexed excerpts of the official docs page. Viewer role could give counsel read access (inference); no approver-type workspace role exists in docs.

claim: Policy Guard provides 'centralized control over permissions and roles across projects within an organization' — org-wide baseline policy rules enforced consistently across environments/projects; 'Only a workspace Owner can add or remove new guarding policy rules'; currently API-only (UI on roadmap); supports RBAC and ABAC, ReBAC forthcoming.
notes: Governance guardrail preventing drift of environment policies from an organizational baseline — structurally similar to a 'mandatory regulatory floor' pattern (inference).

claim: Public REST API at api.permit.io/v2/ (EU region: api.eu.permit.io) covering schema, facts, elements, environments, members etc.; bearer-token auth with three API key scopes (Organization, Project, Environment — environment keys required for PDP containers); documented API rate limits: schema writes 40 req/min, member requests 50 req/min, all requests 1,000 req/min, HTTP 429 on excess.
page_title: Permit API — Getting Started (keys, base URL, rate limits) | Permit.io Documentation
notes: Versioned base path (/v2/) evidences API versioning; no idempotency-key mechanism documented anywhere found.

claim: Cloud PDP enforces built-in per-IP rate limits over 1-minute windows — e.g., /allowed at 1,000 req/min and bulk operations at 200 req/min, returning HTTP 429 when exceeded; container/edge PDP has no such documented caps.
notes: Also documents that Cloud PDP decision logs flow to Permit Cloud 'in the same format as logs from the container PDP.'

claim: SDKs for Node.js, Python, Go, .NET, Java, Ruby (plus beta PHP, Kotlin, Erlang, C++) covering check, bulk check, user/tenant/role/resource management, relationship tuples, condition sets, and permission queries; a Terraform provider exists but 'is not a full SDK.'
notes: Docs candidly list per-SDK feature gaps (e.g., Ruby role-assignment gaps).

claim: Official Terraform provider manages resources/actions, roles, user sets, resource sets, condition set rules, ReBAC relations/role derivations, and user attributes as code — 'version control your authorization policies, automate deployments, and maintain consistency across environments.'
notes: Together with GitOps, the full policy/config surface is exportable and reproducible as code.

claim: Trust Center: SOC 2 Type II with 'latest SOC 2 Type II renewal in January 2026' (sections 1-2 public, full report on request); HIPAA safeguards with BAAs available; GDPR support incl. SCCs and data-subject rights; TLS in transit, encryption at rest with AWS KMS-managed keys.
notes: Compliance-report access is gated to Enterprise plan per pricing page; no ISO 27001 claim found.

claim: Public pricing: Community free-forever tier (1,000 MAU, 20 tenants, 3 environments, unlimited projects, '14 days' audit log retention, community Slack support, no SSO, no compliance reports, all policy models and Elements included); Enterprise tier custom-priced with no MAU/tenant/environment limits, SSO, custom SLA options 'including 0.9999% SLA' [sic — 99.99%], multi-cloud/on-prem, HIPAA BAA/GDPR/CCPA/SOC2 reports, dedicated CSM and professional services; 'No Blackout Features' policy.
notes: Middle (Startup/Pro) tier not rendered in fetched page; see PERMITIO-044. Free-tier audit retention of 14 days is the only concrete retention number published.

claim: Official case studies: Maricopa County Recorder's Office (government — 'increase security and process automation for millions of Maricopa County voters'), Honeycomb Insurance ('two weeks to move from our in-house solution to production'), Hipp Health (healthcare FGA), Centauri AI (fintech — 'one day to implement... one more day to deploy'), Salt Security, Rivulis ('saved us 30% of our valuable development time'); testimonials from Epsagon/Cisco and TechSource Inc. (US DOE contractor).
notes: Vendor-published case studies; demonstrates production use in government/insurance/health/fintech contexts but all are app-authorization use cases, not regulatory decisioning.

claim: Permit.io raised an $8M Series A (Feb 2024; ~$14M total across 2 rounds per Tracxn); press reported 20+ signed companies including Accenture, Cisco, Schneider Electric, SignifyHealth (CVS), and Salt Security.
page_title: Permit.io Raises $8M in Series A Funding — FinSMEs
notes: Indicates a small, early-growth vendor; enterprise logos real but company scale is startup-stage.

claim: Authorization data (users, roles, tenants, resource instances, attributes) is loaded via UI, API ('a fully API-driven backbone'), or JIT at check time; 'Permit automatically pulls in details about users, roles, and more from its cloud database to the PDP's policy engine'; OPAL's Scope Config API can fetch data from external sources directly into PDPs, 'using data without needing to share it with Permit's control plane'; 'no practical limits on number of objects or object sizes' with PDP sharding for very large datasets.
notes: Stateful authz-relevant context is first-class; there is no event history/aggregation store (no counters like 'entries this week') — computed state must be supplied as attributes (inference).

claim: Permit explicitly scopes itself out of identity: 'Authentication (AuthN) is the process of verifying user identity' vs 'Authorization (AuthZ) determines what authenticated users can do'; Permit 'is designed to integrate seamlessly with any authentication solution you already use' and performs no identity verification itself.
notes: Positive scope-boundary evidence used for 0-scores across E-series verification/signal squares: identity, age, address, device, VPN, fraud-scoring capabilities are outside the product's stated scope.

claim: Hybrid architecture separates control plane (Permit cloud: policy configuration, relationships between authorization entities) from data plane (customer VPC: PDP + 'all the actual data required to make authorization decisions'), so 'No sensitive data leaves your network/cloud'; OPAL Server pushes updates to PDP-embedded OPAL clients 'as diffs' in real time.
page_title: How does Permit.io work? | Permit.io Documentation
notes: Decision-making continues if Permit cloud is unavailable (decisions local to PDP); control-plane SaaS dependency is for management, not runtime.

claim: Custom policy escape hatch: customers can write custom Rego (package permit.custom) or Cedar alongside generated code — e.g., deny rules that override UI-generated allow rules ('custom code enables special conditions that override other policies', such as time-window restrictions on a tmp-admin role) — with the caveat 'Extending custom policies with Permit.io is an advanced task, and you should do it at your own risk.'
notes: Arbitrary logic (including obligations/priorities) is achievable in raw Rego/Cedar but outside the managed UI model.

claim: Permit.io achieved conformance with the OpenID AuthZEN request/response protocol in the working group's interop results (announced May 2024), and its CEO Or Weis is quoted as an early backer; the PDP exposes AuthZen-compatible evaluation endpoints.
page_title: AuthZEN Work Group Announces Authorization Interop Results — OpenID Foundation
notes: Standards alignment reduces switching costs between AuthZen-conformant PDP vendors (inference); PDP AuthZen endpoints also documented at docs.permit.io/concepts/pdp/overview/.

claim: Strategic direction: 'AI Access Control' with a Four-Perimeter Framework (prompt filtering, RAG data protection, secure external access with machine identities for agents, response enforcement), an MCP Gateway, and 'traceable, auditable access requests and approval flows' enabling human sign-off for sensitive AI-agent actions.
page_title: Fine-Grained Permissions for AI-Powered Applications | Permit.io
notes: Company R&D focus is visibly shifting to AI-agent authorization, not regulatory/compliance content (inference from positioning).

claim: Webhooks exist for: Elements events (e.g., new user created, approval granted/denied — with shared-secret validation and HTTPS guidance) and PDP data-sync errors ('define a webhook to make Permit notify you when PDP data synchronization issues occur'); no general-purpose webhook for policy-change or per-decision events is documented.
notes: PDP sync-error webhook documented at docs.permit.io/api/pdp-webhooks/. Absence of decision-event webhooks is from search coverage, not an explicit denial.

claim: Observability: official differentiator checklist lists OpenTelemetry support, structured logging, and Datadog integration for the PDP, plus two audit-log surfaces (Permit-side decision logs and API-based activity monitoring).
notes: Container PDP logs can be forwarded to customer logging stacks; Cloud PDP lacks direct metrics endpoints (per cloud-pdp-capabilities page).

claim: Market perception in reviews/roundups: praised for ease of use, the policy editor ('robust enough for developers... simple enough for business users'), responsive community; criticized for 'limited flexibility for dynamic permissions' in some setups; GitOps, custom policies, and Terraform available in free tier.
page_title: Permit.io Review: An In-Depth Look At The No-Code Authorization Platform — StackInsight
notes: Third-party review sites of uneven quality; used only for perception, not capability scoring.

claim: The managed policy model is allow-based (role/action/resource grants and condition-set allows); no rule priority, ordering, or conflict-resolution mechanism is documented in the UI model — deny-overrides and precedence require hand-written custom Rego/Cedar (labeled inference from the policy-basics grant model plus the custom-policy page's positioning of deny rules as custom-code-only).
notes: INFERENCE flag: conclusion derived from two official docs (policy-basics, gitops/custom_policy) rather than an explicit statement.

claim: Permit's documented product surface (docs IA: Model Policies, Enforce Permissions, Work with Data, Manage SDLC, Connect Your App, Embeddable Components, AI Security/MCP Gateway) and all product pages contain no promotion/sweepstakes administration, no marketing-campaign features, no wallet/ledger/stored-value features, no legal content library, and no regulatory monitoring — the product is domain-neutral authorization infrastructure (labeled inference from enumeration of the full documented feature set).
notes: INFERENCE flag: basis for 0-scores in A-, most C-content, E-signal, and F-series squares — grounded in the complete docs table of contents plus homepage/pricing/customers pages reviewed in this ledger, not mere absence of a single mention.

claim: ABAC conditions are built from typed attributes plus comparison operators — documented examples include equals, greater-than (user.age {'greater-than': 40}), between (user.age {'between': [15, 18]}), in (environment.location {'in': ['US','Canada']}), and (ref) operators comparing resource attributes to user attributes — combined with logical allOf/anyOf/or nesting in condition groups.
notes: Compiled from official operators/building-conditions docs surfaced via search excerpts plus the building-abac-policy page (fetched directly, incl. resource.time > '17:00' example). Age/location conditions are enforcement-side only; Permit verifies neither.

claim: Permit CLI includes policy bootstrapping from templates, AI assistance, and OpenAPI specs ('Policy - AI, Templates, OpenAPI'), i.e., technical starter templates exist, but no domain/jurisdiction policy-pack library (legal or regulatory content) is offered anywhere in the product.
page_title: Policy - AI, Templates, OpenAPI | Permit.io Documentation
notes: Title and scope from official docs surfaced via search; page not deep-fetched. Supports J09=1 (technical templates only).

claim: Access Request element: end users request access to restricted resources/roles from inside the customer app; requests are 'sent for approval by an admin (or any other Level 1 role defined in the User Management Element)' who can approve or deny; approvals grant the necessary permissions; requires connection to the User Management element where approvers 'view a list of all pending access requests.'
notes: Approval events observable via Elements webhooks; long-term approval history persistence beyond audit-log retention is not documented.

claim: A self-serve Startup tier introduced Nov 2024 'supports applications with up to 10,000 users, starting at $150 per month', combining an MAU model with resource quotas — bridging free Community and custom-priced Enterprise.
page_title: Permit.io Introduces New Pricing, Bringing Accessible Fine-Grained Authorization to Startups — Business Wire
notes: Company press release; tier not rendered in the pricing-page fetch (JS-loaded), so exact current quota details (e.g., audit retention days for this tier) unresolved.
